high_priority_articles.full_text:
STRASBOURG — The EU will not ease sanctions on Russian fossil fuels even after the U.S. struck a diesel deal with Moscow, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday morning.
In a speech to EU lawmakers, she warned “Russia is not a trusted supplier of energy because it would, this is our experience, at any time weaponize energy dependencies to blackmail others,” arguing it was Russia that cut gas supply to Europe. “That is a lesson Europe certainly will not forget.”
Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on imports of diesel fuel until April 2027, as global oil prices surge.

high_priority_articles.title: UK CBAM 2027: Indicative Figures Show a Lighter Burden Than the EU Regime - IndexBox
high_priority_articles.summary: UK CBAM 2027: Indicative Figures Show a Lighter Burden Than the EU Regime  IndexBox
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The UK Government has released indicative figures for calculating its national Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which is scheduled to take effect in 2027, according to Eurometal. An analysis of the published data indicates that the UK regime will be substantially less stringent and less costly for importers of metal products than the comparable mechanism operated by the European Union.
Simplified methodology
The central distinction is the UK approach of using a simplified methodology. Whereas the EU requires importers to track emissions at the level of detailed HS codes or else face strict default penalty values tied to specific countries, the UK is adopting sector-wide and global averages.
The UK CBAM rate is derived with reference to the volume of free allowances allocated to domestic producers under the national emissions trading scheme, known as the UK ETS. The indicative rate has been set at 9.69 pounds sterling per tonne of CO2.
Default emission figures for the UK are calculated for individual product categories but are averaged across all trading partners, without a breakdown by country of origin. They are based on EU data adjusted to reflect the structure of UK imports, excluding imports from the EU.
Diverging cost burden
A comparison of the financial burden under the two systems points to a wide gap. European steelmakers have raised concerns that a soft Brexit would turn Great Britain and Northern Ireland into a transit hub for circumventing the EU's high carbon tariffs.
At a summit planned for November, the UK and the EU intend to discuss integrating their emissions trading systems and providing mutual exemptions from the CBAM. Looking toward 2029, London is considering aligning its rules with those of the EU, including a shift toward country-specific emissions targets.
Domestic industry concerns
British businesses fear that a domestic CBAM could harm the country's manufacturing sector. The UK's plan to introduce its own CBAM in 2027 has numerous shortcomings and could accelerate the decline of British manufacturing, according to these concerns. Industry groups maintain that the UK Treasury, which is responsible for introducing the carbon tax, has not heeded their concerns and is developing a mechanism that would place British manufacturers at a disadvantage.

high_priority_articles.summary: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine  Euronews.com‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal  Al JazeeraTrump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going  BBCTrump: Zelensky never wanted to end Ukraine war  The TelegraphTrump’s Push for Deals With Russia Powers His Frustration With Ukraine  The New York Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.
Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal."
"He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."
Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.
On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss."
"We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it."
"It's time to make a deal," he said.
Zelenskyy's Oslo talks
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.
Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.
Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."
"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.
In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."

high_priority_articles.title: Tanzania and World Bank Map Central Corridor Investment Opportunities in Agriculture, Logistics, Mining, and Tourism - TanzaniaInvest
high_priority_articles.summary: Tanzania and World Bank Map Central Corridor Investment Opportunities in Agriculture, Logistics, Mining, and Tourism  TanzaniaInvest
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Tanzania and the World Bank are identifying Central Corridor investment opportunities in agriculture, mining, tourism, and logistics, while UNDP prepares projects for a June 2027 investment conference.
The Minister for Finance, Ambassador Khamis Mussa Omar, met the Managing Director of Operations at the World Bank, Anna Bjerde, in Bangkok, Thailand, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Annual Meetings held from 12 to 18 October 2026.
The talks focused on accelerating economic development through infrastructure construction, job creation, and private sector investment, with Omar stressing that progress should be measured by higher production, wider employment opportunities, and rising incomes rather than growth indicators alone.
The meeting also discussed the Central Corridor as a key transport route able to strengthen regional trade, ease the movement of goods, and connect Tanzania’s markets with neighbouring countries.
Omar described tourism as a sector able to create jobs quickly, noting that opportunities around the great lakes and along the coast remain underused and should be developed to raise tourist arrivals and open more employment.
Bjerde said job creation is the World Bank’s top priority in supporting economic development, and that the Bank is advancing a strategy to strengthen micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which account for a large share of business activity and employment.
To support this, the two sides discussed shifting small business lending from reliance on asset collateral towards assessment of business cash flow, so that firms obtain capital according to their capacity to generate revenue, grow, and add jobs.
Bjerde also commended Tanzania’s focus on building an industrial economy through agriculture, livestock, and mineral value addition, a strategy that aims to keep more of the value of national resources inside the country and reach a 40% value addition target.
On education, the World Bank urged a focus on quality and learning outcomes rather than enrolment numbers alone, including better teaching methods and education systems that use artificial intelligence to prepare young people for the global economy and labour market.
World Bank officials said they intend to speed up project preparation and implementation by cutting the time needed before projects start, and the Bank is drafting a special plan to identify and remove the bottlenecks that delay delivery.
Both sides agreed to continue their strategic partnership to accelerate Tanzania’s development priorities, and the Bank encouraged the Government to keep presenting its development needs with confidence so that cooperation and support can be used effectively.
The World Bank Vice President for Eastern and Southern Africa, Dr. Ndiamé Diop, the Minister for Finance of Zanzibar, Dr. Juma Malik Akil, the Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, Dr. Natu El-Maamry Mwamba, and the Permanent Secretary in the President’s Office for Planning, Dr. Tausi Kida, also attended the meeting.
In a separate meeting in Bangkok, Omar held talks with the Administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Alexander De Croo, a former Prime Minister of Belgium, on youth employment, education, investment attraction, and private sector growth.
Omar said youth employment is a key development priority because young people make up a large share of the population, which calls for strategies that equip them with skills, capital, technology, and markets to become self-employed or employable.
“Employment and youth issues are very broad. We need to ensure that young people gain the right skills, affordable start-up capital, technology, knowledge, and access to markets so that they can participate fully in production and national development,” Omar stated.
Omar added that the Government will keep investing in education and education infrastructure to meet demand from population growth, which continues to raise requirements for schools, teachers, books, and other facilities.
He explained that Tanzania continues working with development partners to identify investment opportunities and prepare projects able to attract domestic and foreign investors.
The Government and the World Bank are currently mapping trade and investment opportunities along the Central Corridor, which links the Port of Dar es Salaam with the interior through transport infrastructure including the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), with potential to extend the opportunities to Rwanda.
“This corridor has great opportunities in the agriculture, mining, tourism, and transport sectors and in the development of transport and supply centres (logistics centres), which can attract investment and stimulate production as well as employment,” Omar noted.
Omar also said the Government is improving the business and investment environment, including through recommendations from committees formed to examine challenges in the tax system and in the conduct of business.
De Croo expressed UNDP’s readiness to keep supporting Tanzania’s development agenda, including empowering young people, strengthening skills, and expanding economic opportunities in partnership with the Government, the private sector, and other development institutions.
He said investment should be viewed as a long-term development strategy, particularly in the use of natural resources, including rare minerals needed for the global energy transition.
De Croo commended the Government for preparing the Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF), which he said will help improve the availability and coordination of resources for financing development priorities.
He explained that UNDP, together with the Tanzania Investment Growth Facility (TIGF), aims to turn the identified opportunities into projects backed by documented plans and robust financial and commercial structures able to attract investors ahead of the investment conference expected in Tanzania in June 2027.
“We are ready to work with Tanzania in preparing for that conference and in seeking financing for sustainable infrastructure and blue economy projects through partnership with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), with the aim of accelerating project implementation and increasing the contribution of investment to economic growth and the prosperity of citizens,” De Croo stated.
The meeting was also attended by Akil, Mwamba, the Permanent Secretary in the Zanzibar Ministry of Finance, Aboud Hassan Mwinyi, and Enock Koola, a Member of Parliament and member of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Budget, alongside other Government and UNDP officials.
The Central Corridor is Tanzania’s main transport and trade route, connecting the Port of Dar es Salaam with the interior and with landlocked markets including Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda, Zambia, Malawi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
In August 2026, the Government and the World Bank finalized technical preparations for KAZI MPA, the Catalyzing Jobs and Resilient Growth in the Central Corridor Multiphase Programmatic Approach, which targets youth employment and private sector-led growth along the route.
During a visit to Tanzania that included talks on 20 August 2026, Diop said the Bank’s next phase of cooperation would aim to transform the corridor from a transit route into a fully fledged economic corridor.
TIGF is a platform hosted by the Economic and Social Research Foundation (ESRF) and supported by UNDP to strengthen project preparation, mobilise capital, and fast-track investment in priority sectors, and it was launched during the Tanzania Investment Summit 2026 held in Arusha on 1 and 2 June 2026.
At that summit, the Government presented 60 investment-ready public projects worth USD 6.35 billion, up from USD 2.85 billion at an earlier stage.

high_priority_articles.summary: AfCFTA: Ghana exported to 47 African countries in 2025  CitiNewsroom.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The National Coordinator of the National AfCFTA Coordination Office, Dode Seidu, has underscored the benefits of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), citing Ghana’s export of non-traditional goods to 47 African countries in 2025 as evidence of the country’s progress under the trade agreement.
Speaking on the Citi Breakfast Show on Wednesday, October 21, Mr Seidu said Ghana had made significant strides in implementing the agreement through initiatives across the public and private sectors, although more work was needed to maximise its benefits.
He explained that Ghana was the first country to establish a national coordination office to support the implementation of the agreement, which requires several government agencies and institutions to integrate AfCFTA into their operations.
According to him, various institutions have since taken steps to align their activities with the agreement, demonstrating the country’s readiness to expand trade and investment across the continent.
Mr Seidu cited the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre’s establishment of an AfCFTA focal desk to facilitate and attract intra-African investment as one of the measures supporting the initiative.
“If you go to Ghana’s Promotion Authority, which are all agents under the Ministry of Trade, you’ve seen clear signals. For example, if you look at the annual export NTE non traditional export report issued by Ghana’s for promotion authority in 2025, we exported to 47 African countries under the AFCFTA.”
Despite these developments, Mr Seidu cautioned that significant work remained, particularly in expanding awareness of the agreement among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
He noted that many SMEs were yet to understand the opportunities available under AfCFTA, making it necessary to intensify efforts to educate businesses and encourage their participation in the continental market.

Japanese and South Korean stocks rebounded in early trading on Wednesday, October 21, with semiconductor leaders helping lift both markets as investors assessed overnight U.S. earnings developments.
South Korea’s KOSPI opened 2.05% higher at 5,666.34. Japan’s Nikkei 225 opened up 1.26% at 64,885.95 before extending its advance to 1.41%, reaching 64,979.50.
The recovery gathered pace in Seoul. By 9:30 a.m. Korea Standard Time, the KOSPI had climbed 3.62% to 5,753.55, showing that buying continued beyond the opening jump.
The distinction matters for readers following the session: the initial 2.05% increase represented the KOSPI’s opening move, while subsequent reports captured a stronger intraday recovery. Neither figure represented the closing result.
The early gains suggested renewed appetite for technology exposure. However, the performance of a single morning session provides limited evidence about whether the recent pressure on the sector has ended.
South Korean memory manufacturers were among the main beneficiaries of the recovery.
Samsung Electronics initially gained 2.72%, while SK Hynix advanced 3.92%. Both extended their gains as the morning progressed, rising approximately 6% and 7%, respectively, by 9:30 a.m. local time.
In Japan, Kioxia climbed 5.18% in early trading, while SoftBank Group rose 3.56%.
The simultaneous advances placed memory and AI-related companies at the centre of the regional rebound. Their performance also made sector breadth an important consideration: sustained gains across more companies would provide stronger evidence of improving sentiment than a rally concentrated in a few large names.
For market participants, the immediate question is whether buying can persist through the session and into subsequent trading days. Strong opening moves can reflect improving expectations, but they can also lose momentum as investors reassess valuations and upcoming results.
Fresh figures from Super Micro Computer provided a more concrete development for investors assessing AI infrastructure demand.
The company estimated revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion for its fiscal first quarter ended September 30, above its previous guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. It attributed the increase primarily to stronger demand for AI platforms.
Supermicro also estimated gross margins of 12.0% to 12.5%, compared with earlier guidance of 10.4% to 10.8%, citing customer and product mix.
The update offered evidence that demand could translate into both higher sales and better margins at an AI server supplier. That combination may support sentiment toward the wider infrastructure supply chain.
However, the figures remain preliminary and unaudited. Supermicro said its final results could differ as it completes its financial closing procedures.
The update also cannot establish the earnings outlook for every semiconductor company. Individual suppliers face different product mixes, customer relationships and production costs.
U.S. extended-hours trading showed that investors continued to distinguish sharply between corporate results.
SpaceX shares rose more than 8% later in the after-hours session following stronger-than-expected quarterly results. Supermicro also rallied sharply after its preliminary business update.
Netflix moved in the opposite direction, falling approximately 6% after its earnings release.
The streaming company reported quarterly earnings of $0.87 per share, above the $0.82 consensus estimate, while revenue of $12.87 billion matched expectations. Nevertheless, a reduction in its advertising revenue outlook raised concerns about future growth.
The contrasting reactions illustrated why an earnings beat alone may provide limited support for a share price. Investors also assess guidance, the durability of revenue growth and how much optimism is already reflected in valuations.
For Asian technology shares, the positive AI-related updates offered a supportive backdrop. Netflix’s decline nevertheless showed that company-specific disappointments could still generate substantial selling.
The Asian rebound followed a mixed U.S. regular session on Tuesday, October 20.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to close at 52,495.88. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to 7,712.57, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.02% to 26,424.82.
Strong corporate earnings supported the broader market, while a retreat in oil prices helped equities recover from earlier weakness. However, declines in several large technology companies limited the Nasdaq’s performance.
That divergence matters when interpreting Wednesday’s Asian gains. The overnight session offered support from broader equities, but U.S. technology stocks had yet to demonstrate a uniform recovery during regular trading.
Subsequent after-hours advances therefore represented a further shift in sentiment, rather than a continuation of an across-the-board technology rally.
Attention now turns to additional corporate results, including Tesla and Meta Platforms, and what their updates reveal about spending, profitability and growth expectations.
For semiconductor investors, the central issue remains whether investment in AI infrastructure can produce sustainable revenue and earnings across the supply chain. Strong demand announcements help, but margins and financial returns remain equally relevant.
The breadth of the Asian rebound will also matter. Continued participation beyond Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and a small group of Japanese technology names could strengthen the recovery. A narrow advance would leave index performance more dependent on a handful of stocks.
Japan and South Korea’s early gains marked an improvement in technology sentiment, supported by rising semiconductor shares and encouraging U.S. corporate updates. Whether that recovery lasts will depend on subsequent earnings, buying beyond the opening session and further evidence that AI demand can support profitable growth.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Summary
- MUFG expects the Bank of England to hike by 25bp on November 5 and again in February to a 4.25% peak, saying rising energy costs will push UK inflation above 4% while firm growth, a steadier labour market and sticky underlying prices limit patience.
A hike on November 5 would extend the energy-driven tightening seen across central banks. Any guidance pointing to a February follow-up would likely support sterling, particularly against currencies where central banks are seen as slower to respond. Gilts look the more vulnerable asset: 10-year UK yields already sit at the top of the G7 range, and further tightening alongside reduced fiscal headroom ahead of the Budget could keep pressure on longer-dated debt. For equities, higher rates and energy costs weigh on domestically focused UK stocks, while the FTSE 100’s energy-heavy constituents offer some offset. Oil and gas remain the key swing factor: with household energy bills driving the expected rise in inflation, any further spike in prices linked to the Middle East war would strengthen the case for a longer hiking cycle.

---
MUFG says the Bank of England cannot look through this energy shock the way it might like, because the UK economy is simply too strong to make waiting look safe.
Summary:
- MUFG expects the Bank of England to raise rates by 25 basis points at its next meeting, with another hike in February to a 4.25% peak
- UK headline inflation is seen rising above 4% in coming months as higher energy prices feed through to household bills
- Energy prices have stayed elevated for longer than expected and have risen further in recent months, MUFG says
- A stabilising labour market, healthy growth and elevated underlying inflation leave the Bank of England struggling to look through the shock
- MUFG says UK Q3 GDP is tracking at about 0.65% quarter on quarter, and it forecasts growth of 1.5% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, above IMF projections
- Higher borrowing costs may have cut fiscal headroom to around £15 billion ahead of the Budget
The Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates at its next meeting, as higher energy prices push UK inflation back above 4%, according to MUFG, which expects a further increase in February.
In its European macro and market outlook, MUFG said it expects a 25 basis point hike at the Bank of England’s next policy decision, due on November 5, followed by another in February, taking Bank Rate to a terminal level of 4.25%. The bank said energy prices have remained elevated for longer than anticipated and have moved higher in recent months. As those costs feed through to household bills, it expects headline inflation to rise above 4%.
MUFG argued that the Bank of England will struggle to look through the energy shock, as it might otherwise, because of the wider economic backdrop. The labour market is stabilising, growth is healthy and underlying inflation remains elevated. Services inflation measures are still running well above the Bank’s 2% target.
The UK economy has been notably resilient. MUFG said recent activity data have consistently surprised to the upside, and the economy does not appear to be repeating the second-half slowdowns of recent years, with third-quarter GDP tracking at about 0.65% quarter on quarter. It forecasts growth of 1.5% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, more optimistic than the IMF, despite energy-related headwinds.
That growth is fairly narrow, however, led by professional services and other knowledge-intensive sectors. MUFG said it is too early to draw firm conclusions, but the UK’s comparatively rapid adoption of artificial intelligence could help explain recent productivity gains. The share of UK job postings mentioning AI has risen faster than in the US or major European economies.
The fiscal backdrop is a complicating factor. MUFG estimates that higher borrowing costs may have reduced the government’s headroom against its fiscal rules to around £15 billion. It expects the upcoming Budget to include some offsetting tax measures alongside temporary, targeted support for households facing higher energy bills. MUFG questioned whether reducing fiscal buffers is prudent while growth holds up and geopolitical uncertainty remains high.
The Bank of England’s decision is due at 12:00 GMT (07:00 US Eastern time) on November 5.

high_priority_articles.title: Interest rate hike ‘firmly on table’ after inflation rises to 11-month high - Brentwood Live
high_priority_articles.summary: Interest rate hike ‘firmly on table’ after inflation rises to 11-month high  Brentwood Live
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Inflation rising to the highest rate in almost a year makes it more likely that the Bank of England will hike interest rates next month, with living costs set to rise further this winter, economists think.
Experts have said the latest inflation data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) has reinforced expectations of a rate hike in November.
The ONS said Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation was 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August.
This was the highest rate in 11 months and above the level that economists had been forecasting for the month.
It means the price of goods and services across the economy are rising at a faster rate than they were before, and inflation is drifting further away from the Bank of England’s 2% target rate.
A major driving force of higher inflation last month was motor fuel prices, which rocketed by 30% in the year to September, the latest figures showed.
Petrol and diesel prices have been surging since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran which has squeezed global oil and gas supplies and driven up wholesale prices.
Living costs are expected to rise further in the months ahead as households face higher energy bills this winter.
Many economists are therefore expecting the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month to keep a lid on inflation and stem the risk of so-called “second-round effects” emerging, meaning things such as higher wage demands.
Martin Sartorius, lead economist for the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said September’s inflation rise means an interest rate hike was “firmly on the table” at the Bank’s next meeting in November.
He said the rate-setting committee will likely want to “guard against the risk of persistently higher headline inflation becoming embedded in future wage and price-setting behaviour”.
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist for Deutsche Bank, said further rises in energy prices were “inevitable” and that ongoing tensions in the Middle East were delaying the likelihood of inflation coming down.
He is expecting rates to rise in November and then again in the months ahead.
Nevertheless, Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis for AJ Bell, pointed to a “silver lining for households” in that food prices were “relatively stable” last month.
Food and drink inflation remained the same, at 1.3% in the year to September, and prices fell by 0.2% between August and September.
But the ONS pointed to some experts who say competition between supermarkets to attract shoppers and resist increasing prices is keeping a lid on inflation, but this could be harder to maintain in the future.
“The knowledge that funding our lives is only going to get harder in the coming months will impact consumer confidence,” Ms Hewson said.
“If they can, people will look to pad out savings, but they’ll also postpone big ticket purchases and will be looking to the Government to step in when times get tough.”
Chancellor John Healey, who is due to deliver his autumn Budget statement next week, has said he will “look to do more” to provide “breathing space” on living costs.
He said: “People can see prices rising. They see it at the pumps. They see it in their bills.
“They see it with monthly mortgage costs, and they can see it’s driven by the conflict in the Middle East.
“We’re a week away from the Budget, and I think if people look at what we did in the first week of the Government – £2 cap on bus fares, we cut VAT off electricity bills, we reduced business rates for pubs, clubs, and venues.
“And I will look to do more, as I can, to give a bit of breathing space on the costs of living and the costs of business at the Budget.”
Meanwhile, the September inflation rate is typically used to decide the level of increase for many benefits, such as universal credit, tax credits and disability benefits.
This rate is also a key part of the pension triple lock, which is used to decide how much pensions will increase by in the following April.
But the increase is based on either this inflation rate, average earnings growth between May and July, or 2.5%.
State pensions are, therefore, widely expected to increase by 3.9% next year based on wage growth figures which is the highest of the three.
The data also showed that Consumer Prices Index including Housing (CPIH), the ONS’s preferred measure of inflation, rose to 3.6% in September from 3.3% last month.
Retail Prices Index (RPI) inflation rose to 3.9% from 3.4% in August.

high_priority_articles.summary: Dollar-Yen Stuck in Upper 157 Range as FOMC, BOJ Meeting Keep Trading Rangebound  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The dollar-yen pair continues to lack direction in the Tokyo foreign exchange market. After trading in the lower-to-mid 158 range following a mild bout of yen selling versus the prior week's close, the pair remains caught between official pushback and intervention caution from Japanese and U.S. authorities on the upside, and firm U.S. rates and high crude oil prices on the downside. Market participants are broadly positioning for a range of roughly 157.50-159.00 yen while watching three key catalysts: next week's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, the Bank of Japan's policy meeting, and the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
In late New York trading last week, the yen finished at 158.45-55 per dollar. Persistent U.S. inflation concerns weighed on the yen as long-term Treasury yields rose 0.07 percentage point from the prior week's close to 5.14%. With September U.S. consumer price index (CPI) and producer price index (PPI) data both pointing to accelerating inflation, markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to hold policy rates steady at its October 27-28 FOMC meeting before raising rates at its December meeting. Rising energy prices also supported yen selling. Front-month WTI crude settled at $103.66 a barrel, up 2% from the prior week's close, heightening concerns about the negative impact on Japan's economy through higher import costs.
Even so, the dollar's upward momentum and the yen's weakness remain limited. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said at an October 16 press conference that the underlying inflation rate is "broadly near 2%, and we cannot tolerate it rising further." At the Upper House Budget Committee session on October 19, he also indicated that if short-term rates are not adjusted appropriately and market concerns about upside inflation risks grow, "long-term interest rates could rise." Expectations for additional rate hikes are a factor supporting yen buying, but views remain entrenched that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's fiscal expansion path could worsen Japan's fiscal position, and yen buying momentum has not been sustained.
On the yen side, comments from senior government officials are also being watched as trading cues. Finance Minister Katayama said on October 21 that the economy is shifting from import-price-led inflation to inflation accompanied by wage growth, expressing the view that there is no gap between the government's and the BOJ's policies. If yen weakness continues to push up import prices, expectations for BOJ policy normalization could again spur yen buying. Meanwhile, in phases where the dollar-yen pair holds at elevated levels, caution over yen-buying intervention by the government and BOJ tends to cap the upside.
Technically, the upside and downside targets are relatively clear. On the upside, the 200-day moving average at 158.56 yen and the recent high of 158.95 yen come into view, while on the downside, the October 19 low of 157.70 yen and the daily Ichimoku cloud's baseline at 156.95 yen are seen as support levels. Yoshio Iguchi of the Dealing Section in Traders Securities' Market Division assumes a range of roughly 157.50-159.00 yen and expects the pair to continue failing to extend in either direction, positioning the near term as a phase of trading within the range while gauging the next catalyst ahead of next week's FOMC and BOJ meetings and the U.S. midterm elections.
The euro is also lacking direction amid a dearth of fresh catalysts, much like the dollar-yen pair. In France, the spread between French and German 10-year bond yields has exceeded the symbolic 150 basis point level amid fiscal deterioration and political uncertainty, with wariness seeping into the government bond market. Even so, euro selling has lacked momentum in the foreign exchange market, with views emerging that bad news is already largely priced in and that accumulated short euro positions make additional selling difficult. The euro has been trading centered on the $1.12 level against the dollar, and its downside remained limited even as concerns about political and fiscal management reignited following large-scale protests and riots across France.
What market participants are watching most closely is the direction of U.S. interest rates. This week offers few high-profile U.S. economic indicators, with weekly jobless claims and October PMI results likely to shape the outlook for the economy and inflation. If U.S. rates rise again, that would support the dollar-yen pair, while continued rate declines would tend to strengthen dollar selling. Heightened Middle East tensions and high crude oil prices support safe-haven demand for the dollar, but improved investor sentiment following U.S. tech company earnings works in the direction of weakening dollar buying as a safe-haven asset.

The stalemate in the currency market directly affects Japanese companies' export profitability and import costs, making it impossible for commercial participants to ignore. Further yen weakness would increase household burdens through higher import prices while providing a tailwind for exporters. However, the difficulty of the pair moving in one direction amid intervention caution from the government and BOJ is making it harder for companies to set their assumed exchange rates. Some market voices say the range could break depending on the outcomes of the FOMC and BOJ meetings, with yen buying potentially accelerating especially if the BOJ proceeds with an additional rate hike. Some also see the U.S. midterm election results shaping the direction of fiscal policy, and investors are poised to carefully assess the market's direction after these events pass.

Meerut to Get ₹200-Crore Critical Minerals and Rare Earth Refinery, 1,300 Jobs Expected
The proposed facility will recover critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel from used lithium-ion batteries
Uttar Pradesh is set to strengthen its position in advanced materials recycling with a proposed ₹200-crore critical minerals and rare earth refinery in Meerut. Deep-tech startup Circulogy Cleantech Private Limited has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Invest UP for the proposed project.
The facility is expected to generate approximately 300 direct and 1,000 indirect employment opportunities, taking the anticipated employment impact to around 1,300 jobs. The project is planned to be developed in phases, with a targeted annual processing capacity of 10,000 tonnes at full scale.
The refinery will focus on recovering valuable materials from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries, electronic waste and used permanent magnets, helping convert discarded products into resources for industrial use.
Lithium, Cobalt and Nickel Recovery in Focus
The proposed facility will recover critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel from used lithium-ion batteries. These materials are essential for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage systems and several electronics applications.
The project also envisages recovering rare earth elements, including neodymium, dysprosium and terbium, from discarded permanent magnets used in electronic equipment, hard drives and electric vehicle motors.
Rare earth elements are important for high-performance motors, renewable energy technologies, electronics and several strategic applications. Developing domestic recovery capabilities could help India diversify its sources of these materials and strengthen its recycling ecosystem.
Boost to India’s Critical Minerals Strategy
India’s growing electric vehicle, renewable energy and electronics industries are increasing the importance of securing reliable supplies of critical minerals. Dependence on imported materials remains a strategic concern for manufacturers and policymakers.
The proposed Meerut refinery could contribute to domestic mineral recovery by extracting valuable materials from products that would otherwise enter waste streams. Such facilities can complement conventional mining by recovering resources already present in batteries, electronic equipment and industrial components.
The project also aligns with the broader policy push to strengthen India’s critical minerals value chain, including exploration, processing, recycling and the recovery of materials from end-of-life products.
However, the project’s eventual contribution to reducing import dependence will depend on its commissioning, actual recovery rates, feedstock availability and the commercial scale of operations.
Invest UP to Facilitate Project Development
The MoU with Invest UP is intended to facilitate the proposed investment and support the company in navigating applicable approvals and clearances. Assistance in accessing relevant central and state government incentives may also be available, subject to eligibility and prevailing rules.
The project represents an opportunity to expand technology-led industrial activity in western Uttar Pradesh. Critical mineral recycling combines waste management with resource recovery, creating potential opportunities for specialised processing, logistics and associated industrial services.
1,300 Employment Opportunities Expected
The proposed investment is expected to create around 300 direct jobs and 1,000 indirect jobs. The indirect employment impact could extend to supply chains, collection and transportation of used batteries and electronic waste, and supporting industrial services.
The targeted capacity of 10,000 tonnes per year would position the proposed facility as a significant recycling project, provided it achieves its planned scale of operations.
The next milestones will be the development of the facility, completion of necessary approvals, commissioning and the commencement of commercial operations. These stages will determine when the anticipated employment and industrial benefits begin to materialise.
For Uttar Pradesh, the project signals an opportunity to participate in the emerging market for critical mineral recovery and advanced materials recycling, an area of growing importance to India’s manufacturing and clean-energy ambitions.

high_priority_articles.title: Japan says rare earth yttrium supplies have stalled amid China export controls - Malay Mail
high_priority_articles.summary: Japan says rare earth yttrium supplies have stalled amid China export controls  Malay Mail
high_priority_articles.full_text:
TOKYO, Oct 21 — Global exports of the rare earth yttrium have stalled, causing what a Japanese official described as a “supply-demand crunch”, with the Financial Times reporting that Tokyo was months away from running out of the critical metal.
Yttrium is essential for manufacturing consumer electronics, LEDs, aviation engines, semiconductor production equipment and a variety of industrial products.
China accounts for almost two-thirds of rare earth mining production and 92 per cent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency.
“It is true that exports of yttrium have stalled not only to Japan but worldwide, causing a supply-demand crunch and soaring prices,” a Japanese industry ministry official told AFP today, on condition of anonymity.
“Exports to Japan have decreased, including delays in shipments, and the global volume itself is low,” the official said.
The comments came after the Financial Times reported that Japan could exhaust its supply of the critical material in “months”.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in July that yttrium was “globally scarce” and was “an important rare earth for our country”.
According to Chinese customs data, exports of yttrium oxide to Japan amounted to 4,000 kilograms in September, compared with 51,000 kilograms in the same period the previous year.
The industry ministry official said Tokyo was working with the United States and European nations on critical mineral resources and rare earths, including yttrium.
Beijing has intensified pressure on Tokyo since Takaichi hinted last November that Japan could intervene militarily in any attack on self-ruled Taiwan.
China views Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out taking it by force.
“China imposed export controls on Japan in accordance with laws and regulations, with the aim of curbing Japan’s attempts at remilitarisation and possessing nuclear weapons,” Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing today.
Japan has asked the US government and American businesses to press China to ease rare earth export controls to avoid “severe disruption to the global automotive, defence and chip industries”, the Financial Times report said.
US defence supply chains rely on Japanese components that use yttrium, the newspaper said. — AFP

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Accordingly, following the direction of the Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc in Official Letter No. 9136/VPCP-CN dated September 8, 2026, from the Government Office, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is currently drafting a Decision to amend and supplement several articles of Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg dated May 29, 2025, of the Prime Minister regulating the structure of retail electricity tariffs (draft Decision) using a simplified procedure to soon apply the retail electricity tariff structure stipulated in Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg and the peak, off-peak, and normal hours of the national power system as stipulated in Decision 963/QD-BCT dated April 22, 2026.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade is seeking feedback on amendments to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg on the structure of retail electricity tariffs.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade has recently issued Official Letter No. 8615/BCT-DL dated October 19, 2026, to relevant parties requesting their input on the draft Decision amending and supplementing several articles of Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg.
The draft Decision amends regulations related to the effective date of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg to promptly apply a new retail electricity pricing structure and peak/off-peak hours to align with the current load profile of the power system.
Article 1 of the draft Decision abolishes the continued application of Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg. According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the current retail electricity pricing structure and peak/off-peak hours are still applied according to the regulations in Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg and the Circular guiding Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg. This abolition corresponds to the full implementation and application of the provisions of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg as stipulated in Article 2 of the draft Decision.
The draft Decision also amends and supplements the provisions in Clause 1, Article 7 concerning the effective date of Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg, stipulating that Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg takes effect from a specified date (to be determined when the Prime Minister signs and issues the amending and supplementing Decision), removing the phrase "applicable from the date of the most recent adjustment of the average retail electricity price after the effective date of this Decision" so that the entire content of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg takes effect and is applied in practice from the effective date of the amending and supplementing Decision.
At the time the amended and supplemented Decision takes effect, the entire Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg is replaced by Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg and the amended and supplemented Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg. Therefore, the retail electricity tariff structure will be applied according to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg, and the new peak and off-peak hours will be applied according to Decision 963/QD-BCT from the date the amended and supplemented Decision takes effect.
Clarify the electricity tariff structure for industrial customers with voltages of 220 kV and above.
The draft Decision also replaces the phrase "220 kV voltage level" with the phrase "Voltage level from 220 kV and above" in section 1.1.1 of the Appendix attached to Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg to clarify that the retail electricity tariff structure in section 1.1.1 of the Appendix to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg applies to manufacturing customers purchasing electricity from a voltage level of 220 kV and above.
Explaining this amendment, the Ministry of Industry and Trade stated that in its submission No. 2318/TTr-BCT dated April 3, 2025, to the Prime Minister regarding the draft Decision on the structure of retail electricity tariffs, the retail electricity prices were explained according to voltage levels as follows: high voltage above 35 kV (including voltage levels above 35 kV to below 220 kV and voltage levels of 220 kV and above), medium voltage from above 1 kV to 35 kV, and low voltage below 1 kV; In fact, in the calculations to determine the retail electricity tariff structure stipulated in Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg (replacing Decision No. 28/2014/QD-TTg), the retail electricity tariff structure for customers purchasing electricity at 220kV voltage level is also the retail electricity tariff structure for customers purchasing electricity at voltage levels above 220kV.
Therefore, according to the calculations in Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg, customers purchasing electricity at 220kV voltage level will have the same price as customers purchasing electricity at voltage levels of 220kV and above. This is also the method used to determine the retail electricity tariff structure in Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg, according to which Section 1.1 of the Appendix attached to Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg stipulates the retail electricity tariff structure applicable to manufacturing customers at "Voltage levels of 110 kV and above".
“Replacing this phrase helps ensure consistency when applying the retail electricity tariff structure to manufacturing customers, avoiding misunderstandings and preventing the exclusion of certain groups. This is not a new policy or regulation, but rather a policy or regulation that was proposed when drafting Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg, consistent with the calculation of the retail electricity tariff structure in Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg,” the Ministry of Industry and Trade emphasized.
In addition, the draft Decision also amends and supplements the note on the application period of the retail electricity tariff structure for electric vehicle charging in the Appendix to Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg to conform with the effective date and application of the entire amended Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg.
Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg stipulates that the retail electricity tariff structure for electric vehicle charging will be applied for a period of 3 years from the date the retail electricity tariff structure under Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg is actually applied as stipulated in Clause 1, Article 7 of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg. Accordingly, the new structure will only be applied from the date of the first adjustment of the average retail electricity price after Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg comes into effect.
Due to the effective date and application of Decision 14/2025/QD-TT, which has been amended and supplemented as mentioned above, the application period of the retail electricity tariff structure for electric vehicle charging also needs to be adjusted accordingly.
Once the Draft Decision is signed and comes into effect, the retail electricity pricing structure in Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg and the new peak and off-peak hours stipulated in Decision 963/QD-BCT dated April 22, 2025 will be applied immediately.
However, the Ministry of Industry and Trade noted that the immediate application of the new retail electricity pricing structure is not a one-time adjustment of the average retail electricity price. The average retail electricity price remains unchanged at the current rate of VND 2,204.0655/kWh, as stipulated in Decision 599/QD-EVN dated May 7, 2025, of EVN on adjusting the average retail electricity price.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The 19th Semiconductor Day commemorative ceremony was held on the 21st. Semiconductor Day was established to mark October 29, 1994, when South Korea’s annual semiconductor exports first surpassed 10 billion dollars. Thirty-two years later, this year, South Korea’s semiconductor exports exceeded 340 billion dollars as of September. The 10 billion dollars in exports from 1994 now equates to just ten days’ worth of semiconductor exports today. The starting point of South Korea’s now-giant semiconductor industry was a personal investment of 500,000 dollars thrown into a venture company on the brink of bankruptcy. It was the late Lee Kun-hee, Samsung chairman, who injected 500,000 dollars of his personal funds to acquire a 50% stake in Hankook Semiconductor in December 1974, six years before his passing on the 25th, which marks the sixth anniversary of his death this year.
Established in early 1974, Hankook Semiconductor was South Korea’s first private wafer-processing company. However, it faced bankruptcy within less than a year. Lee Kun-hee, then 32 years old and a director at Tongyang Broadcasting (TBC), used his personal funds to acquire the stake. Opposition within Samsung was strong, with critics arguing, “Pursuing high-tech industries is reckless when we can’t even make TVs properly.” But he later reflected, “During the oil shock, I realized that a country without natural resources could only survive through high-tech industries created by the mind.” That Hankook Semiconductor became the foundation of Samsung Electronics’ current semiconductor (DS) division.
There was no original technology. Overseas consulting firms and U.S. and Japanese semiconductor companies recommended starting with non-memory chips for home appliances or simple assembly and processing, which required less initial capital. However, Lee Kun-hee insisted on a “direct push into memory chips,” betting on lowering costs through large-scale equipment investments to compete in the global market. To persuade his father, Lee Byung-chul, the founder, who favored a cautious approach of testing every step, he frequently compiled and submitted data. He also invited Japanese engineers to South Korea every weekend to acquire technology. As a result, on February 1983, Lee Byung-chul officially declared Samsung’s entry into semiconductors in Tokyo—eight years after acquiring Hankook Semiconductor’s stake. In December that year, Samsung became the third company in the world, after the U.S. and Japan, to successfully develop a 64K DRAM. However, losses continued, with the company losing 1 dollar per chip sold.
During the development of the 4-megabit DRAM in 1987, a debate erupted between the “stack method” of layering circuits upward and the “trench method” of etching substrates downward—neither of which U.S. or Japanese companies had solved. Lee Kun-hee, then vice chairman, decisively ended the debate by stating, “We go with the stack method.” He judged that the simpler structure would be advantageous for mass production and defect correction. While Japan’s top company, Toshiba, which chose the trench method, struggled with mass production yield issues, Samsung, which maximized productivity with the stack method, dominated the DRAM market. Lee later said, “I had a hunch the stack method was right, but I wasn’t 100% sure. We were lucky.”
The decisive blow to widen the gap was preemptive investments even during downturns. In 1993, he introduced an 8-inch wafer line, which had double the production capacity of the then-standard 6-inch wafers, when competitors hesitated due to technical burdens. This investment allowed Samsung to rank first in global memory semiconductor sales in October that year. Even when DRAM prices plummeted due to the dot-com bubble collapse in 2000, he pushed for the world’s first transition to 12-inch wafers. His urging of the hesitant Samsung management to “hurry up” and invest paid off.

high_priority_articles.title: How Duty Drawback Can Help Recover the Cost of Forced-Labor Tariffs - Supply Chain Brain
high_priority_articles.summary: How Duty Drawback Can Help Recover the Cost of Forced-Labor Tariffs  Supply Chain Brain
high_priority_articles.full_text:
On July 24, 2026, a new set of Section 301 tariffs took effect that few supply chains can sidestep. Following investigations opened on March 12, 2026, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative asserted that dozens of trading partners were failing to impose or enforce bans on goods made with forced labor.
The response was sweeping. The action covers all products from roughly 60 economies, including Canada, Mexico, the European Union, United Kingdom, China, India, Japan and Switzerland, at an added rate of either 10% or 12.5% depending on the country of origin.
For importers, the immediate concern is cost. These are additional duties, and for most goods they’re layered on top of the rates that importers already owe. There are exemptions, and USTR added hundreds of products to that list before the effective date, covering items such as certain seeds, fertilizer and pesticide inputs, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, pharmaceuticals and used clothing. Even so, the majority of goods from the listed economies now carry the extra charge.
It's worth being precise about what these tariffs are. They’re trade-remedy duties assessed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. They’re not the same as the forced-labor import prohibitions enforced under Section 307 of the Tariff Act or the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which stop non-compliant goods at the border entirely. The Section 301 tariffs apply to goods that are admissible and lawfully entered. That distinction matters, because duties paid on lawfully entered goods can often be recovered later. Goods barred from entry cannot.
The recovery mechanism is duty drawback, which refunds up to 99% of the duties, taxes and fees paid on imported merchandise when that merchandise, or a qualifying substitute, is later exported or destroyed. It’s one of the oldest programs in U.S. trade law, created so that goods passing through the U.S. on their way to a foreign market aren’t permanently burdened by U.S. import duties.
Section 301 duties are eligible for drawback. This sets them apart from Section 232 steel and aluminum duties and Section 201 safeguard duties, which are not recoverable through drawback, and from antidumping and countervailing duties, which are also excluded. Because the new forced-labor tariffs are Section 301 duties, importers who export can pursue a refund on the portion of their goods that leaves the country.
The most direct route is unused merchandise drawback. If a company imports a product, pays the Section 301 duty, and then exports or destroys that product without using it in the U.S., it can claim back up to 99% of the duty. The goods don’t have to be the exact ones imported. Substitution rules let a company match imports and exports that share the same eight- or 10-digit Harmonized Tariff System classification, which adds flexibility for busy operations.
The second route is manufacturing drawback. Here, a company imports components or raw materials, uses them to produce a finished article, and exports that article. The duties paid on the imported inputs, including the Section 301 charge, become recoverable once the finished product is exported. This is common in industries that bring in parts and ship out assembled goods.
Both paths reach back further than many importers expect. A drawback claim can generally cover imports from the previous five years, so duties already paid on past entries aren’t necessarily lost.
Many companies affected by the forced-labor tariffs aren’t simply selling into the U.S. market. They re-export, supply foreign customers, and run global manufacturing that moves goods back out of the country. For those flows, drawback turns a portion of the new tariff from a sunk cost into a refund. It doesn’t erase the tariff, and doesn’t apply to goods consumed domestically, but on the exported share it can return nearly the full amount.
A few practical points. Documentation is everything. Customs and Border Protection reviews drawback claims tied to Section 301 duties closely, and clean records that link specific imports to specific exports are what carry a claim. Antidumping and countervailing duties on the same goods remain off the table. And, because eligibility turns on specifics such as classification, export evidence and timing, a review of your own import and export history is the only reliable way to assess the opportunity.
The forced-labor tariffs are broad, and will remain in force while the legal challenges filed against them work through the courts. Classification review and exemption checks belong in any response. So does drawback, which for exporters is often the single largest lever available to recover what these new duties add at the border.
Tony Nogueras is founder and chief information officer of Alliance Drawback Services.

Britain's annual inflation rate accelerated by more than expected in September, rising to 3.5% on surging fuel prices. This comes a week before the UK government presents its autumn budget and as UK public sector net debt tops £3 trillion.
Annual consumer price inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in September 2026, its highest since October 2025, from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
The higher-than-expected reading comes one week before the Labour government presents its annual budget on 28 October, which is expected to address cost-of-living pressures.
The rise was largely driven by fuel price increases. Average diesel prices in September reached their highest level since July 2022, as the US-Iran war sent petrol and diesel prices soaring.
Transport, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution to the change in annual inflation, the ONS said. Transport prices rose by 6.6% year-on-year, up from the previous month’s 4.6%.
Annual services inflation accelerated to 3.7%. Housing and household services and communication costs rose by 5.3% and 5.8% year-on-year, respectively. Food inflation was unchanged at 1.3%.
Core CPI inflation increased to 2.8% from 2.6%. Compared with August, consumer prices rose 0.4%, following a 0.5% increase.
“The energy price cap rose slightly in October, with households braced for an even larger hike early next year," said Danni Hewson, AJ Bell head of financial analysis. He added that expectations are influenced by rising service costs, as well as the significant increase in the price of raw materials that businesses use to produce, on top of the jump in the cost of transporting those goods.
"The knowledge that funding our lives is only going to get harder in the coming months will impact consumer confidence," Hewson said.
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates at its next meeting on 5 November, which could be the first such move since 2023. This could follow increases by the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve amid renewed inflation pressures.
"Market expectation of a November increase is now nearing 100%, with more than a 50% chance that a second hike will follow before the end of the year,” Hewson said.
The UK central bank's current benchmark rate is 3.75%, against an inflation target of 2%.
UK borrowing rises as public debt surpasses £3 trillion
In a separate release, the ONS said that public borrowing was nearly £25 billion (€29.8 billion) in September 2026.
UK public sector net borrowing totalled £24.5bn (€29.2bn) in September, £1.8bn (€2.1bn) more than a year earlier, surpassing market expectations.
The higher borrowing comes as "spending, including higher debt interest costs, increased more than government income, partly reflecting the impacts of inflation", the ONS said.
This comes as a recent global bond sell-off has driven up bond yields, making borrowing more expensive for leading economies including the US, France, Germany and the UK. UK 10-year gilt yields were just below 5.4% at the end of September, having reached a 19-year high earlier that month.
Meanwhile, UK government borrowing between April and September 2026 reached £97.8bn (€116.5bn), slightly below the same period last year and the equivalent of 3.1% of gross domestic product (GDP). The amount was still £6bn (€7.1bn) more than the Office for Budget Responsibility's forecast.
Public sector net debt at the end of September 2026 was provisionally estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion (€3.57 trillion) for the first time. However, as a proportion of the economy, debt was lower than a year earlier, the ONS said.
Debt stood at 94% of GDP, down from 94.7% a year earlier.

high_priority_articles.summary: Bank of Japan Projected to Maintain Quarterly Rate Hikes to Contain Inflation Risks  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The Bank of Japan is likely to raise its benchmark interest rate every three months as it works to anchor inflation around its 2 percent target, according to a former senior central bank official. The projected trajectory underscores a definitive shift from the country's prolonged era of monetary easing, driven by persistent price pressures and a tightening domestic labour market.
Eiji Maeda, a former Bank of Japan executive director who previously oversaw monetary policy, indicated that the central bank will probably continue normalising its policy at a steady, predictable pace. Maeda, who currently serves as the president of the Chibagin Research Institute, expects the next rate increase to occur in December, followed by another move in March or April.
"The pace has now accelerated to roughly one hike every three months, and I think that's appropriate," Maeda said in a Bloomberg interview on Tuesday. He noted that the central bank must balance the need to contain inflation with the risk of fuelling excessive market expectations regarding the speed of monetary tightening.
The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25 percent in September, following an earlier increase in June. The successive moves marked the fastest pace of monetary tightening the institution has undertaken since 1990. The September adjustment brought the policy rate into the estimated range of a neutral rate—defined as the level that neither stimulates nor restricts economic growth—which is believed to sit between 1.1 percent and 2.5 percent.
Calibrating the Neutral Rate
According to Maeda, if the midpoint of around 1.75 percent is taken as a benchmark, the central bank's policy rate could reach a neutral stance by next spring. He suggested that the Bank of Japan might eventually be compelled to lift its benchmark rate to 2.25 percent, which would require approximately four more quarter-point increases.
The overnight index swap market aligns broadly with this outlook, indicating that investors assign a roughly 80 percent probability to a rate hike by December. However, the central bank is widely expected to hold rates steady at its upcoming policy meeting on October 30.
Maeda cautioned that executing back-to-back hikes at consecutive meetings carries significant risks. "If the BOJ delivers back-to-back hikes, markets may increasingly expect another consecutive move," he explained, adding that the central bank has strong reasons to avoid such a scenario unless forced by a sharp depreciation of the yen.
Dismantling the Easing Framework
The current tightening cycle represents the dismantling of the Bank of Japan's complex and aggressive easing framework, which defined the institution's approach for over a decade. Under previous leadership, the central bank implemented a negative interest rate policy and a yield curve control mechanism designed to pin 10-year government bond yields near zero.
These unconventional tools were intended to shock the economy out of a deflationary mindset. However, as global interest rates surged in recent years to combat inflation, the Bank of Japan's commitment to ultra-low rates placed immense downward pressure on the yen. The growing disparity between Japanese and international yields forced the central bank to incrementally adjust its yield curve control parameters before finally ending the negative rate policy entirely.
Maeda, who played a key role in the central bank's initial monetary response to the COVID-19 pandemic, previously argued that maintaining the 10-year peg was only viable in a global environment of low interest rates and low inflation. The shift toward a standard interest rate framework allows the central bank to respond more conventionally to economic data.
"As underlying inflation approaches 2 percent and financial conditions remain accommodative, failing to adjust our policy rate appropriately could push up long-term interest rates by stoking market concern over an inflation overshoot," Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament earlier this month. The governor emphasised that raising rates at a measured pace helps prevent sudden, disruptive spikes in bond yields.
Inflation Drivers and Policy Assessment
A central focus of the upcoming October policy meeting will be whether Governor Ueda and the policy board conclude that underlying inflation has sustainably reached the 2 percent target for the first time since the goal was established in 2013.
While Maeda does not expect the central bank to explicitly declare the target achieved, he noted that a modest upgrade to the bank's inflation assessment would not be surprising. Recent data supports a firmer inflation profile; headline inflation climbed to 2.1 percent in September, while the core measure—excluding fresh food and energy—stood at 2.3 percent.
Governor Ueda recently reinforced the central bank's vigilance, stating that policymakers "cannot tolerate" underlying inflation rising further above the 2 percent threshold. Speaking in Bangkok following a gathering of global finance chiefs, Ueda confirmed that underlying inflation is already near the target level.
The central bank has identified several primary drivers sustaining the current inflationary environment:
- Wage-Price Dynamics: A historically tight labour market is forcing companies to increase compensation, creating a positive loop that supports domestic consumption and allows firms to pass costs to consumers.
- Global Technology Demand: Surging demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure is boosting domestic capital expenditure and driving export growth.
- Currency Volatility: Prolonged periods of yen weakness have periodically increased the cost of imported raw materials and energy supplies, adding external price pressures.
As the Bank of Japan prepares to release its latest economic projections, market participants will closely scrutinise the language surrounding the inflation outlook. While the immediate policy setting is expected to remain unchanged, the groundwork is being laid for a sustained cycle of quarterly rate increases as Japan definitively closes the chapter on decades of deflationary stagnation.

UK inflation strengthened again in the autumn. The UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) reported on Wednesday that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August, above the economists' consensus estimate of 3.4%, and the highest reading in the past year. CPIH, which includes owner-occupiers' housing costs, rose 3.6% year-on-year in September.
This marks the third consecutive month of rising UK CPI. After 2.9% in July and 3.1% in August, the further jump in September effectively wiped out the disinflation gains hard-won in the spring. The ONS noted that motor fuel inflation hit its highest level since August 2022 — the period when the full-scale Russia-Ukraine conflict broke out and international oil prices soared. As of September, UK gasoline and diesel prices were up 29.8% year-on-year, with retail prices at their highest since the summer and autumn of 2022, making transport the largest contributor to overall price growth.
Notably, the momentum was not confined to energy. Core CPI, which strips out food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8%, goods inflation rebounded markedly, and services inflation remained sticky. Although food inflation held at a relatively low 1.3%, industry bodies warned of time lags in cost pass-through, suggesting food price pressures may persist for some time. Cooling prices at hotels and restaurants partly offset the energy-driven increase.

|---|---|
| July 2026 | 2.9% | 
| August 2026 | 3.1% | 
| September 2026 | 3.5% | 
| September 2026 Core CPI | 2.8% | 
| September 2026 CPIH | 3.6% | 
| September 2026 Motor Fuel | 29.8% | 
Note: Core CPI excludes food, energy, alcohol and tobacco; CPIH is the inflation measure that includes owner-occupiers' housing costs.
Scott Gardner, an investment strategist at JPMorgan's personal investing division, said in a report that the recent inflation rebound "has consumed the disinflation gains achieved in the spring." He argued that Bank of England policymakers will not focus solely on the headline inflation figure, and that the acceleration in services inflation in recent months is more worrisome, raising concerns over whether second-round inflation effects have emerged beyond higher energy prices. He added that the current challenge differs from 2021, but ongoing conflict is weighing on the UK economy, making the case for a rate hike more compelling.
Market reaction was relatively restrained. After the data, the pound was roughly flat against both the euro and the dollar, and UK gilt yields moved little, suggesting investors were already prepared for elevated inflation. The real focus shifted to the rate path: interest rate market pricing shows traders see a 98% probability that the Bank of England will raise rates by 25 basis points to 4% next month, with most also betting on another quarter-point increase at the central bank's final policy meeting of the year in December.
As a net energy importer, the UK has always been highly sensitive to external energy shocks; events such as escalating geopolitical conflict in the Middle East or disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz could quickly feed through to domestic fuel and consumer prices. On international comparisons, UK September inflation was higher than in France and Germany, standing out among major European economies.
For investors, the significance of this data lies in the possibility that the Bank of England's policy path may be steeper than previously expected. CPI is the Bank of England's anchor policy indicator, and resurgent inflation will add uncertainty to the rate outlook; if services inflation and wage pressures fail to cool, the probability of a prolonged tightening cycle rises. The pound may find short-term support, but valuation pressure on UK government bonds and rate-sensitive assets will also increase in tandem. The next round of UK inflation data is scheduled for release on November 18, which will be the most critical test before the central bank's December meeting.

high_priority_articles.title: UK inflation hits 3.5% as petrol prices soar: is November rate hike now inevitable? - TradingView
high_priority_articles.summary: UK inflation hits 3.5% as petrol prices soar: is November rate hike now inevitable?  TradingView
high_priority_articles.full_text:
UK inflation climbed to 3.5% in September, its highest rate in almost a year, as soaring petrol prices and renewed pressure on underlying costs increased the likelihood of a Bank of England interest-rate rise next month.
Consumer prices rose 3.5% annually, compared with 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday. Core inflation accelerated to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation increased to 3.7% from 3.4%.
The figures leave policymakers facing a difficult choice: contain a spreading inflation shock or risk adding to the strain on households already paying more for fuel and borrowing.
Petrol surge puts more pressure on household budgets
Motor fuel inflation reached 29.8% in September, up from 23% in August. Petrol averaged 169.5 pence a litre, the highest since August 2022, while diesel reached 192.5 pence, its highest since July that year.
Transport inflation accelerated to 6.6% from 4.6%, making it September's biggest inflation driver.
Higher pump prices hurt households immediately. They also raise distribution and operating costs for businesses, some of which may eventually be passed on to customers.
Researchers led by Huw Dixon at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research warned that inflation could reach 5.4% in early 2027 under its intermediate energy-price model.
That is a scenario, not a consensus forecast, but illustrates how a prolonged oil and gas shock could keep prices rising.
UK inflation: Bank of England faces a tougher November decision
Bank Rate remains at 3.75%. In September, six policymakers favoured leaving rates unchanged while three wanted a quarter-point increase.
Before Wednesday's figures, 54 of 63 economists surveyed last week expected a November rise to 4%.
Tuesday's labour-market report added to the case for tightening. Unemployment unexpectedly fell to 4.7%, while regular pay grew 3.7% in the three months through August.
Bank policymaker Megan Greene argued that economic resilience may mean less spare capacity to contain wage-driven inflation than previously assumed.
Waiting for conclusive evidence of persistent wage and price pressures, she warned, could leave policy responding too late.
Governor Andrew Bailey has offered a more cautious interpretation. In comments reported by the Financial Times last week, he said firms were still largely absorbing energy costs rather than passing them on, although prolonged pressure could change that behaviour.
Higher borrowing costs threaten to compound the squeeze
A November hike would come at a difficult time for consumers. More expensive fuel leaves less room for discretionary spending, while higher mortgage and business lending rates risk weakening demand further.
The picture is not uniformly inflationary. Food inflation held at 1.3%, and price growth at restaurants and hotels eased to 3.8% from 4.1%.
But core and services inflation moving higher together will make it harder for the Bank to dismiss the latest increase as temporary.
The government's October 28 Budget adds another constraint. Elevated gilt yields increase debt-servicing costs and limit room for fiscal support just as households face a renewed cost-of-living squeeze.
